issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

vignette: Amir was twenty-eight when the maintenance crew's work cart slipped on the greased rails of the west yard. He had been walking the perimeter, clipboard in hand, when the guardrail gave way. He watched three men go down into the switch yard's tangle of iron and gravel. What stayed with him was not the sound, but the stillness that followed, and the exact sixty-two degrees of wet chill that had clung to his forearms as he knelt in the gravel, pressing his hands against a colleague's neck where blood had already begun to soak through his flannel. He waited for the ambulances, counting seconds, watching the red darken the gray concrete, feeling the precise thermal signature of that November night embed itself into his skin. He kept a heavy wool blanket in the cab years later, not for warmth, but because the exact temperature of that moment had left a tactile imprint that resurfaced whenever the ventilation fans shifted or the morning dew settled on the platform. When he returned to the depot, the breakroom's climate control felt like a different kind of air, but it was only that specific cold that made his breath catch. When the dispatch supervisor told him the yard was now swept clean and secure, Amir found it impossible to believe the words. He could not trust the assurances; the architecture of safety felt temporary, like the plywood barricades they had erected that day. He stopped relying on the safety briefings. At the same time, he began pacing the platform edges during his shifts, eyes tracking every moving object, holding his body in a state of permanent readiness. He told himself he was just doing his job, but what he was doing was scanning for the next slip, the next fall. By December, his days and his nights operated on the same frequency. At night, he lay on the edge of his mattress with the bedroom lights on, refusing to close his eyes until his body had registered that the deadbolt was engaged and the street outside was quiet. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert. He was certain that if he drifted off, he would miss the moment something went wrong. Over the months, this became the rhythm of his existence, with the hypervigilance of his shifts and the sleep vigilance of his bedroom running side by side. His role as a train conductor meant he spent hours in enclosed cabs and on open platforms, environments that offered little control over what might happen outside his window. When a commuter fainted on the 4:15 express, Amir had been the one to answer the intercom. He watched the paramedics wheel the man out, and the sight of the visible wound on the commuter's knee, the bright red against the pale skin, made his own hands tremble so violently he had to lock the throttle. He never spoke of it. Instead, he began avoiding the east-side platforms, citing mechanical checks, though he knew it was because he could not bear to watch if anyone's clothes tore or if someone fell. His route assignments shifted, and his dispatcher noted his growing reluctance to cover the commuter rush, eventually pulling him from the schedule to prevent a breakdown. He told his friends he was working less to save up for a house, but what he really needed was to distance himself from the sight of exposed skin and the smell of copper. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsteady, a structure that could fracture without warning, and his body had learned to live in that state of fracture. Now, at twenty-nine, Amir sat in the intake room with his hands folded tightly in his lap. The clinic's thermostat was set to seventy degrees, and he focused on the exact warmth of the air against his wrists, waiting for the familiar tightness in his chest to pass. He had finally made the appointment after a scheduled layoff, his supervisor gently suggesting he take leave before he was removed from the roster entirely. He was hoping the therapists here could give him a way to step off the platform edges without feeling like he was falling. What frightened him most was not the past, but the certainty that he would never again trust a room, a route, or a night to be truly safe. He wanted to sleep. He wanted to sit in a cab and feel the train move without counting the seconds. He wanted, above all, to stop waiting for the next accident.
